sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Does each heading name what its section holds?" and "Can a first-time viewer say in one sentence what this piece is for?"**
   - **Where:** The title "River ferry timetable" (about x 120–480, y 75–115) promises a timetable. Below it are three prose paragraphs (y 145–470) and no timetable at all: no departure times and no table.
   - **What the viewer meets:** They come for times, scan for a grid of times, and find a description of the service. To get the one fact they need, they have to work it out from "every forty minutes between early morning and late evening", and in winter from "one boat each hour… before dusk". Even then they can't, because "early morning", "late evening" and "dusk" give no clock times. The page fails the job its own title sets.
   - **Why:** The heading has to describe what's under it (WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.6, Headings and labels). A page should be self-evident and easy to scan within seconds (Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*).
   - **Fix:** Either add the real timetable (first and last departure, the interval, and summer and winter columns) under the title, or rename the page to match what it holds, for example "About the river ferry". Since the title already says timetable, adding the times is the better fix.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect. Major.

**What's working.**
- **One mood throughout.** It uses one sans-serif family, near-black on white, and no decoration. It reads as a single calm, practical public-information notice, which suits a local ferry service.
- **Nothing extra.** There are no rules, boxes or ornaments, so every mark on the page is content.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the times appear somewhere else, such as further down the page, in a linked PDF, or in content that hadn't loaded when the screenshot was taken. The empty right half and lower third could be a missing table. Check the live page. If the timetable does load there, the finding becomes "put the times next to the title".

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (first-time viewer can say what it's for; each heading names what its section holds), 0 unsure

**First read.** The eye goes straight to the bold "River ferry timetable" heading at the top left (about x 120–480, y 75–115), then drops into three paragraphs of the same grey-black body text. It reads as a plain information page for people who ride the ferry. The right half of the canvas, and everything below y≈470, is empty.

**What it's for (my assumption).** A public web page telling riders when the ferry runs and what the rules are.

**Walk (What matters first)**
- One element clearly dominates: yes. The title is about twice the body size and bold.
- Text levels can be told apart at a glance, with no near-same sizes: yes. There are only two levels, the bold title (~36 px) and regular body (~18 px), and the step between them is large.
- Headings differ in more than size: yes. The title is bold and the body is regular.

Every line is yes, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Outside the checklist, for the director: the title promises a timetable, but there isn't one. The facts a rider acts on are buried at the same weight as everything else in the running text: "every forty minutes", "twelve minutes", "one boat each hour" in winter, and the last crossing "before dusk". The type hierarchy is sound, but the information under it is flat. A rider scanning for when the next boat leaves gets no level that pulls out times or frequency. The fix is to lift those key times out of the prose into their own clearly marked level, or into an actual timetable. This is a defect of content and structure (common sense, no catalog entry), and it is probably major for the page's job. It may belong under whole or text rather than here.

**What's working.**
- The title-to-body step is large (about 2×) and backed by weight. That makes a clean two-level scale with no near-miss sizes, so the start point is obvious.
- The title and body share one left edge (x≈120), so the drop from heading into reading is direct.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. Also covers **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over…?**, which I answered no. All the content sits in one block in the upper left (x≈120–735, y≈75–470). The right ≈45% of the frame (x≈735–1280) and the bottom ≈40% (y≈475–800) are empty. Together they make one large L-shaped void that is unexplained. The page looks unfinished and tips toward the top left, as if a column or a picture failed to load. The title makes this worse: it promises a *timetable*, and the empty right column is just where a reader would expect one, so the eye goes looking there and finds nothing. Why: a heavy side needs a counterweight (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, "Balance"), and empty space should be shaped on purpose, not left over (Tschichold, *The New Typography*; Ruder, "Form and counter-form"). Fix: give the empty space a job. Put the actual timetable (times, landings, winter schedule) in the right column on the same top line as the title, so it balances the text. If this really is a text-only page, size the frame or the measure to the content, or centre the column in the page container, so the empty space reads as margin and not as a gap. If the right column holds content that did not render in this capture, the finding reduces to checking that it loads. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- One firm left edge at x≈120. The title and all three paragraphs share it exactly, with no near-misses, so the column reads as a single deliberate unit.
- The spacing steps are clear. Title to first paragraph is ≈30 px, paragraph to paragraph ≈20 px, and line spacing is ≈27 px. The title sits with its text, the paragraphs read as separate but related, and the measure stays around 70–75 characters.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Whether the empty right column is a timetable or other content that did not load in this capture. Check the live page. If something renders there, re-judge the balance.
- How the single column behaves at wider and narrower viewports: whether it stays pinned left or centres.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (visual weight balances; empty space gathered and deliberate), 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye goes to the bold heading "River ferry timetable", then to three calm paragraphs in a narrow left column. The right half and the bottom third are empty. It reads as an information page for ferry passengers. Assumed job: tell riders when and how the ferry runs.

Text: body large enough yes (about 18 px). Captions yes (there are none). Plain upright face yes (a sans like Inter). One type plan yes. Small text weight yes. Contrast yes (near-black on white). Text over image yes (none). Line length 45–75 yes (about 65–73 characters). Leading yes (about 1.5). Multi-line heading yes (one line). Flush left yes. Justified yes (none). Rag yes, gently uneven. Widows/runts yes ("the boat.", "the side of the deck.", "the coming week." are each several words). Heading breaks yes. Paragraph marks yes (space only). Left edge crisp yes. Chunking yes (three short paragraphs). Mixed case yes. Emphasis yes (none). Display spacing tighter yes (heading looks slightly tightened). Kerning yes. Text tracking yes. Caps letterspaced yes (none). Ligatures yes (no fi or fl in large type). Faux styles yes. Quotes/dashes yes (none). Tabular figures yes (no number columns). Real type yes. Nothing clipped yes.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
None.

Outside the checklist, on the copy (for the director to weigh): the heading promises a "timetable", but the page gives no times. It says "every forty minutes between early morning and late evening", "before dusk" and "one boat each hour" with no first or last departure and no clock times. Then it sends the reader to the printed timetables in the shelters. A rider who opens this page to catch a boat can't plan from it, and the times are what they would act on. This is a defect. Weight: major for the piece's job. Fix: give the actual first and last sailings for each season, or a real table of times, or rename the page so it doesn't promise a timetable.

**What's working.**
- **The paragraphs are easy to read.** Body text is about 18 px in a plain sans, with lines of roughly 65–73 characters, about 1.5 line spacing, and near-black on white. It reads comfortably, and nothing in the setting slows the reader down.
- **The text is broken into short pieces.** There are three short paragraphs, each on one topic (the route, bicycles, winter), separated by space only. A reader can find the bicycle rule without reading everything else.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**First read:** The eye lands on the bold heading "River ferry timetable" at the top left, then moves down three paragraphs of dark gray text on white. The right half of the page and the bottom third are empty. It reads as a plain information page for passengers: calm, neutral, with no colour at all.

**Job (assumed):** a web page that tells ferry passengers how the service runs.

**Walk: Color**
- Small palette: yes. One neutral range (near-black text on white) and no hues.
- Strong colour kept to a small share: yes. There is no saturated colour.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Dark text on white gives a full value range, and the structure reads the same in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool recedes: yes. No temperature is used.
- Matching colours look the same: yes. Heading and body share the same dark gray wherever they sit.
- Neighbouring strong colours differ in lightness: yes. There are none.
- Status colours used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not carried by colour alone: yes. Nothing is coded by colour.
- Dark theme on dark gray: yes. This is a light page.

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies. It is a neutral, text-only page, so the lines are answered against a page with no hues.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The text is a soft near-black on white, not pure #000. That keeps strong contrast for reading the three paragraphs (x 120–732, y 145–470) without the harshness of pure black on white. Heading and body share one ink colour, so hierarchy comes from size and weight, not from competing colours.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure
